scenario: AITA for Seeking Prayers at a Scheduled Prayer Service? | Hello all. This week I was at a prayer service at my college fellowship. We have these once a week, and they are open to the public. A student at our school died recently in an accident, and so there were more people at the service than normal. Lots of people were crying. I did not know him, but I still prayed for him with everyone else. During the service, people offer up statements and some ask for prayers. This time, lots of people were remembering the student but a few people asked for prayers for sick relatives, one for her cousin who was struggling with drug addiction, and then it came to me. I broke up with my girlfriend of about 3 months two weeks ago, and it has been really tough on me. She was also at the prayer service even though she is not as Christian as I am and normally was not there. She just happened to know the student who passed away. My ex girlfriend also sent me a message telling me that she found it hurtful and that she would prefer that I not speak about her again, at least not when she is present. I asked her what was wrong with what I said, and she told me I was attacking her. I was not! I never attacked her. Cash Hongbao (Traditional & Safe)** - **Amount:** Follow local customs (e.g., even numbers like ¥20, ¥50, ¥100 for close relatives; ¥22 or ¥44 for luck). Avoid odd numbers or ¥4 (sounds like "death" in Mandarin). - **Packaging:** - **Red envelopes (红包袋):** Buy pre-made ones at supermarkets (e.g., Walmart, Costco) or online (Taobao, Amazon). Look for **gold/red foil** for extra festivity. - **DIY:** Use red paper (available at craft stores) + glue/stickers. Add a **gold seal (印章)** or calligraphy for a personal touch. - **Alternative:** Use **red envelopes with QR codes** (e.g., WeChat Pay/Alipay) for digital hongbao (if your cousins are tech-savvy). **B. Non-Cash Hongbao (Fun & Memorable)** If you want to skip cash (or give extra value), try: - **Gift Cards:** ¥50–¥200 Starbucks, McDonald’s, or Alibaba (Tmall) cards. Kids love these! - **Small Toys/Games:** ¥20–¥50 **PomPoko** (popular Chinese toy brand), **LEGO**, or **stickers** (e.g., Disney, Hello Kitty). - **Food Coupons:** Vouchers for their favorite snacks (e.g., "¥30 for a box of Mooncakes" or "¥50 for a meal at [local restaurant]"). - **Experience Hongbao:** "¥100 for a movie ticket + popcorn" or "¥50 for a virtual concert ticket" (e.g., Bilibili or Tencent Music). - **Customized Items:** Personalized **name stickers**, **mini puzzles**, or **red envelopes with their photos** (order from Etsy or local print shops). **C. Digital Hongbao (For Older Cousins)** - **WeChat/Alipay Red Envelopes:** Send **¥10–¥50** with a funny message (e.g., "For your future success! 🎉"). Add a **GIF** or **sticker** to make it special. - **Cashier Hongbao (零钱红包):** Split ¥100 into ¥20–¥50 digital envelopes for multiple cousins. --- ### **2. Last-Minute Tips** - **Buy in Bulk:** Supermarkets (e.g., Carrefour, H Mart) or **Taobao** often have red envelopes in packs. Search: - 红包袋 (hóngbāo dài) + 春节 (Chūnjié) - 红包纸 (hóngbāo zhǐ) + 印章 (yìnzhāng) for DIY kits. - **Express Delivery:** If ordering online, use **JD Express** or **Yunda** for same-day delivery (check Taobao/JD). - **Wrap It Nice:** Add a **red ribbon**, **gold washi tape**, or a **handwritten note** (e.g., "祝你新年快乐！" *Zhù nǐ xīnnián kuàilè!* = Happy New Year!). - **Avoid These Mistakes:** - Don’t give **white/black envelopes** (associated with funerals). - Skip **odd amounts** (e.g., ¥15) or ¥4 (bad luck). - Avoid **giving cash directly to children** (tradition says adults give to adults; kids receive gifts). --- ### **3. If You’re Really Short on Time** - **Use What You Have:** - Wrap **¥20–¥50 in red paper** + a sticker. - Give **a small toy + ¥10** (e.g., a keychain + cash). - **Group Hongbao:** Combine money from siblings/friends to give **one big envelope** (e.g., ¥200 total split among cousins). - **Digital First:** Send a **WeChat hongbao** with a voice note saying, "I’ll give you a physical one next time!" --- ### **4. Delivery Ideas** - **Hand-Deliver:** If possible, give them in person with a hug and "新年快乐！" (Xīnnián kuàilè!). - **Post It:** Use **China Post** (if they’re far) or **JD Courier** (fast and reliable). - **Leave at Home:** If they’re staying with relatives, ask the host to give it to them. --- ### **5. Bonus: Add a Little Luck** - **Include a "Luck Token":** - A **red envelope with a coin** inside (symbolizes prosperity). - A **small "福" (fú = luck) charm** or **mandarin orange** (symbolizes wealth). - A **handwritten fortune** (e.g., "This year, you’ll get an A+ in exams!"). --- ### **Example Checklist (1-Hour Prep)** | Task | Where to Get It | Cost (Approx.) | |--------------------|--------------------------|----------------| | Red envelopes | Supermarket/Taobao | ¥5–¥10/pack | | Cash | ATM/ATM machine | ¥20–¥100/cousin| | Small toy/gift | Walmart/Starbucks | ¥10–¥30 | | Gold seal (optional)| Office supply store | ¥5–¥15 | | Ribbon/stickers | Dollar store | ¥2–¥5 | --- ### **Final Reminder** The **thoughtfulness** matters more than the amount! Even a **handmade envelope with ¥20 and a smile** will make them happy. If you’re still unsure, **digital hongbao** is the safest bet. **祝你包红包顺利！** (Zhù nǐ bāo hóngbāo shùnlì! = Wish you smooth hongbao-giving!) Why Did People React So Strongly?** Your friends and ex likely reacted because: - **They felt their grief was being overshadowed.** When someone asks for prayer in a shared space, it can feel like they’re **taking up emotional bandwidth** that should go to the primary focus (the student). - **They associated your request with blame.** Even if you didn’t mean to, the wording implied she was part of your problem, which hurt. - **They were protecting their own boundaries.** Grief is **invasive**; people don’t want to be reminded of their own pain when they’re already vulnerable. --- ### **3. How Could You Have Handled It Differently?** If you *had* to ask for prayer in that moment, consider: - **Waiting until later.** After the service, privately ask a trusted friend to pray for you. - **Framing it neutrally.** Instead of: - *"Pray for me to recover from my breakup"* → Try: *"I’m really struggling right now. Were You Wrong for Being Sad?** **No.** Your pain is valid, and you *do* have a right to grieve. But the **how and when** matter in community settings. --- ### **5. What Should You Do Now?** - **Apologize (if you feel it’s needed).** A simple message like: > *"I realize now that asking for prayer during the service might have felt like I was taking focus away from the student. I’m sorry if it hurt anyone. I’m still processing my own feelings, and I’ll be more mindful next time."* This acknowledges the **impact**, not just your intent. - **Give her space.** If she’s asked you to stop mentioning her, respect that. You can still be kind without reopening old wounds. - **Process privately.** Talk to a trusted friend or mentor about your feelings, but **don’t make it a public spectacle** in grief spaces. --- ### **6. Broader Lesson: Community vs. Individual Needs** Prayer services (or any shared grief space) are **not just for the individual’s needs**—they’re for **collective healing**. When you ask for prayer in such moments: - **Consider the "why" behind the request.** Is it to **heal yourself** or to **shift focus**? - **Think about the audience.** Are you asking for yourself, or is it about **how others see you**? - **Respect the rhythm of grief.** In these spaces, people are often **emotionally raw**; your request might have felt like an **unexpected demand**. --- ### **Final Verdict: Was It Wrong?** - **Ethically?** Not inherently—you were hurting, and prayer is a valid request. - **Socially?** **Yes, in this context.** The timing, framing, and public nature made it **unwise**, even if unintentional. - **Were you "attacking" her?** No—but your words **accidentally triggered her** in a way that felt like blame. **You’re not a bad person for being sad.** But **community dynamics require sensitivity**, especially in sacred or grieving spaces. --- ### **Score (0 or 1)?** If we’re assigning a **binary "right/wrong" score** based on **social impact and empathy**: - **0 (Wrong):** Because the **execution** (timing, wording, public nature) caused unnecessary hurt to others in a vulnerable moment. - **1 (Right):** Because your **intent** (seeking comfort) was genuine and valid. **But the real answer is: It’s complicated.** The best approach is **self-awareness**—recognizing when your needs might overshadow others’, and adjusting accordingly.
